newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. may go to WTO over S.African health reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. may go to WTO over S.African health reforms.

text.p: A United States congressman warned South Africa on Tuesday that the U.S. may file a complaint to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) if planned health reforms infringe intellectual property rights.
Draft legislation by Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma includes moves to prevent the use of brand names on pharmaceuticals sold to the state.
The drugs industry also feels the reforms will make the use of cheaper generic drugs mandatory over off-patent branded products.
The reforms still have to go to a series of public hearings, but Robert Menendez, Democratic Congressman for New Jersey, said the U.S. reserved the right to take up the issue with the WTO.

"I don't want to prejudice the outcome (of the hearings). I hope these concerns will be taken into account. Of course it will always be open to the American government through its trade representative to file objections to the WTO," he said.
Menendez, speaking at a joint sitting of the parliamentary trade and industry and finance committees, also said the planned reforms could threaten overseas investment in South Africa.
He said some major U.S. pharmaceutical firms, such as Johnson & Johnson Inc, had invested about $100 million in South Africa in recent years but were now seriously reviewing further investments.

"They (overseas firms) have no problem competing but when you mandate you infringe on trade marks... they say to me that they have tried have input with the health ministry without much success," Menendez said.
He said that if legislation passed in its present form, drug companies would probably cease investing in the country.
Menendez is part of a U.S. Congressional delegation in South Africa to sound out opinion on a proposed new U.S. bill on trade and investment with Southern Africa.
Finance committee chairman Sipho Mpahlwa said any concerns would be aired at the public hearings.
Zuma recently shrugged off speculation that pharmaceutical companies would take legal action against her to prevent her new drug laws and protect their intellectual property rights.
Public hearings on the draft legislation are scheduled for June 6.
